name: Bocotá de Chiriquí
confidence_why: Margery Peña's 1996 phonology of the Chiriquí dialect calls it an accentual language of the free-accent type and his 1992 and 1994 text collections mark stress word by word, but he had called the same dialect tonal in 1989, Gunn and Gunn 1974 describe accent at the phrase level, Chevrier 2017 still lists Buglere among the Chibchan languages where tone versus accent has been an open question, and the 1996 article is known only from search excerpt, so lexical stress is the likely answer but it rests on one fieldworker's revised analysis.

catalog_quote: El bocotá de Chiriquí se manifiesta como una lengua acentual. En este plano, el acento constituye el incremento de intensidad que adquiere una sílaba en el marco de una palabra o, como más adelante se verá, en el contexto de una cláusula. La función distintiva del acento queda establecida si acudimos a los siguientes contrastes existentes entre términos bisílabos y, en un caso, trisílabos. Así: /gú.dɛ/ 'comer': /gu.dɛ́/ 'felino' ... /dá.bɛ/ 'rojo': /da.bɛ́/ 'maduro' /dá.gɛ/ 'amargo': /da.gɛ́/ 'palma real' ... /ba.dá.da/ 'ave (genérico)': /ba.da.dá/ 'nieto' [p. 23] Establecido de esta manera el bocotá de Chiriquí como una lengua acentual del tipo de las denominadas "de acento libre", es necesario, en relación con este suprasegmental, hacer una breve referencia al carácter de acentuados y no acentuados que hemos postulado para los términos monosilábicos. [p. 24]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Margery's mature (1992-1996) analysis: Buglere/Bocotá is a stress-accent language, not a tone language; each polysyllabic word heard in isolation has one syllable of intensity prominence (Narraciones bocotás 1992 / Mitología 1994 note, snippet). Where that syllable falls is NOT stated in anything I could open; the Margery 1996 forms reproduced by Chevrier 2017 (pp. 369-372) carry the acute on varying syllables (biúsi, ɡuáɡaba, dái, badá, ɡiɾɔ́ɡɾɔ, daɡɛ́, tãʤuɡádɛ), which is consistent with lexically determined placement but is my inference, not a source statement. The earlier Margery 1989 note (held PDF, p. 72) analysed the same variety as a low-yield two-tone language (high vs low), and Chevrier 2017 lists Buglere among the Chibchan languages where tone vs accent remains an open question.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened text.
new_statements.exceptions: Margery 1994 (snippet): at phrase level the prominence 'no se percibe en algunos términos bisilábicos'. Gunn & Gunn 1974 (snippet) describe a phrase accent (acento de frase, marked ') that is weaker than sentence accent, with final-syllable lengthening as the most consistent phrase cue and four phonological phrase types.
new_statements.domain_note: Margery: word-level prominence in citation forms, with phrase-level reduction; Gunn & Gunn 1974 work at the phonological-phrase and sentence level. Margery 1989 (full text held by the project, p. 72): 'el bocotá -hasta el estado actual de nuestras investigaciones en este campo- se nos ha revelado como una lengua tonal, de bajo rendimiento, con dos tonos fonemáticos, uno alto y otro bajo' — later abandoned by the author.
new_statements.identity_note: All of Margery Peña's work (1988-1999) describes the 'bocotá de Chiriquí' variety (Chiriquí province / Costa Rica border area, informants such as Francisco Rodríguez Atencio); Gunn & Gunn 1974 (SIL) describe Bocotá in central Panama (HLAS: 'some 1,500 speakers located in central Panama and divided..'), i.e. the Bocas del Toro/Veraguas side. Glottolog has no separate dialect codes; both fall under bugl1243. Ethnonym/glossonym variants: Buglere, Bocotá, Bokota, Bogota, Murire, Sabanero.

new_statements.quote: el bocotá de Chiriquí se revela, al parecer, como una lengua acentual. Así, percibido de manera aislada cada término polisilábico contiene una sílaba que se percibe como [prominente]. Sin embargo, en el nivel de la frase tal prominencia culminativa que determinados términos, por lo general disilábicos, presentan, se pierde. [...] para la representación del acento hemos acudido al diacrítico colocado sobre la vocal que en términos tri o tetrasilábicos funciona como núcleo de la sílaba prominente o culminativa tanto en el nivel aislado como en el fraseal. En el caso de los términos mono y disilábicos, la colocación de este diacrítico opera de acuerdo con la acentuación fraseal percibida.
new_statements.translation: Bocotá de Chiriquí reveals itself, apparently, as an accentual (stress) language. Thus, perceived in isolation, every polysyllabic word contains one syllable that is perceived as [prominent]. However, at the level of the phrase, the culminative prominence that certain words, generally disyllabic ones, show is lost. [...] to represent the accent we have used the diacritic placed on the vowel which, in tri- or tetrasyllabic words, functions as the nucleus of the prominent or culminative syllable both in isolation and in the phrase. In the case of mono- and disyllabic words, the placement of this diacritic follows the phrasal accentuation as perceived.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Margery 1996: 'lengua acentual' of the free-accent type, read as lexical/unpredictable): the 1992 book likewise treats the language as accentual with no positional rule and marks stress per word. It adds the phrase-level detail (prominence of disyllables lost in the phrase; mono- and disyllables accented by phrasal accentuation; tri-/tetrasyllables stable) and the hedge 'al parecer'. It does not state a placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts a free-stress claim on its own.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is treated as a stress (accentual) language: in isolation each polysyllabic word has one culminative prominent syllable, whose position is not derived from any rule but marked word by word with an acute accent on its vowel; in connected speech the word-level prominence of many disyllables disappears and mono- and disyllables are accented according to the phrasal accentuation heard, while tri- and tetrasyllables keep the same prominent syllable in isolation and in the phrase. No positional generalization (initial, penult, final) is stated. The full reconstructed passage also says that at phrase level some monosyllables are prominent and others are not ('algunos términos monosilábicos se perciben como estructuras silábicas prominentes, en tanto que otros carecen de esta propiedad').
new_statements.exceptions: Word-level prominence of certain, mostly disyllabic, words is lost at phrase level; phrase-level prominence of monosyllables varies word by word; the authors hedge the accentual classification with 'al parecer' (apparently) and call the alphabet provisional ('de valor manifiestamente provisional', feedC10).
new_statements.identity_note: The 1992 book and all of Margery's statements concern the Chiriquí dialect of Bocotá/Buglere (Panama, Chiriquí province); the phrase 'al menos en este dialecto' in the same passage shows the authors restrict their phonological claims to that variety. Gunn & Gunn 1974 describe Bocotá of central Panama (Veraguas/Bocas del Toro communities) and may reflect a different dialect.

readall_conflicts: The disagreement is chronological within Margery's own work rather than between independent sources: in Scripta ethnologica 1987 and RFL 15(2) 1989 n. 7 (p. 72; also LAIL Speaks! 1990) he described Bocotá de Chiriquí as 'una lengua tonal, de bajo rendimiento, con dos tonos fonemáticos, uno alto y otro bajo'; from ELC 1991 and this 1992 book onward (and Mitología 1994, same wording) he calls it 'al parecer' a stress language, and in 'Fonología del bocotá de Chiriquí' (ELC 15, 1996, p. 24) an accentual language 'del tipo de las denominadas de acento libre'. Gunn & Gunn 1974 (Fonología bocotá, snippets only) describe a phrase accent and a sentence accent rather than word-stress placement, i.e. a phrase-level analysis, and Chevrier 2017 (fn. 6) still lists Buglere among the Chibchan languages for which tone vs. accent is open. None of the accessible sources gives a fixed position for word stress; the 1992 statement does not contradict the catalog's lexical/unpredictable reading.
